Extracting environmental data along tracks

Source: vignettes/articles/extracting-environmental-data-along-tracks.Rmd
extracting-environmental-data-along-tracks.Rmd

A marine observation may describe a journey rather than a single location. A trawl moves through several grid cells during a haul. An animal tracked at intervals may also meet different conditions between its recorded positions. Assigning one temperature to the midpoint can miss this variation.

However, the line connecting two positions is an assumption. We don’t know that an animal followed the shortest route, moved at a constant speed or changed depth steadily. Those choices should be visible in our analysis.

What environmental conditions occur along a trajectory, and how do our sampling assumptions change its summary?

In this tutorial we use extract_to_track() to follow a fictional trawl, compare observed vertices with samples between them, and then explore a dive whose depth and time change. The temperatures come from the same small, real Copernicus Marine subset used in the point extraction tutorial. The trajectories are fictional teaching examples, not observed fishing or animal movements. No downloads or credentials are needed.

extract_to_track() runs three steps, which the workflow article writes out:

  1. Build: as_vector3d() turns the vertices of each track into a line, and sample_3d() places points along it.
  2. Intersect: extract() reads the value at each point, or, with a radius, buffer_3d(), crop(), as_voxel() and mask() keep the values in a buffer around it, and summarise_3d() gives their mean.
  3. Summarise: the values of each track’s samples are summarised, each weighted by the distance or time it stands for.

Environmental values are taken from the grid cell, depth level and time step each sample falls in. They are never interpolated between grid values.

Our research question

Imagine a trawl haul recorded at three locations. We want to describe the deeper environmental conditions along its path, rather than use a single representative point.

Here, method = "bottom" means the deepest model level with a value at each sampled position. It doesn’t establish the actual seabed depth or show that the fishing gear was at this depth.

Getting started: preparing our data

Run the code from the repository’s vignettes/articles/ directory, as when building this article. The example netCDF and its attribution accompany the point article in point-data/. Drawing helpers in buffer-data/ are shared with the buffer tutorial; all extractions use the package’s exported functions.

library(ocean3d)
nc_file <- file.path("point-data", "temperature-points.nc")
source(file.path("buffer-data", "figures.R"))

haul <- data.frame(
  haul = "haul_A",
  lon = c(-0.12, 0, 0.12),
  lat = c(37.96, 38.02, 38.08),
  date = as.Date("2026-09-20")
)
haul
#>     haul   lon   lat       date
#> 1 haul_A -0.12 37.96 2026-09-20
#> 2 haul_A  0.00 38.02 2026-09-20
#> 3 haul_A  0.12 38.08 2026-09-20

Rows are in the order they were travelled; extract_to_track() doesn’t sort a route by date. With several tracks, set track_col to the column that groups the positions into tracks. Each track needs at least two vertices, and a vertex without coordinates is an error, so an unknown gap can’t silently become a connecting segment.

Step 1: Extracting at the recorded positions

First, use only the vertices. Each vertex takes the value of the cell, depth level and time step it falls in, as a point does.

observed <- extract_to_track(
  data = haul, nc = nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  method = "bottom", output_col = "temperature"
)
observed$samples[c("track_id", "sample_id", "lon", "lat", "temperature")]
#>   track_id sample_id   lon   lat temperature
#> 1   haul_A         1 -0.12 37.96    13.80234
#> 2   haul_A         2  0.00 38.02    13.76159
#> 3   haul_A         3  0.12 38.08    13.72215
observed$summary
#>   track_id     mean n
#> 1   haul_A 13.76192 3

The result has two tables:

  • samples: the positions queried, the distance and time each stands for along the track, and their values.
  • summary: one row per track, with the requested statistics and n, the number of samples with a value.

The summary doesn’t replace the individual results. For example, we can save observed$samples as a table and analyse each selected temperature, just as we would after point extraction.

# To save the individual results when running this tutorial manually:
# write.csv(observed$samples, "haul_sample_temperatures.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Step 2: Sampling the path between vertices

sampling sets where values are read:

sampling Positions queried When it is useful
"vertices" Only the recorded vertices; the default without a step. Attach conditions to recorded tag locations without assuming positions in between.
"balanced" Evenly spaced points that meet every step limit; the default with a step. Sample an assumed dive between tag records, limiting changes in kilometres, metres and hours together.
"merged_steps" The evenly spaced points for the distance and depth limits, and separately a point at each time step. Check how adding points at each time step changes the results of a depth-sampled dive.

Every inserted position is on the same assumed trajectory. These modes change where it is queried, not which route the animal is assumed to have followed.

Balanced sampling inserts positions along the connecting route. Here, neighbouring samples are at most one kilometre apart. This distance is a maximum: the function keeps all the vertices and divides each segment into equal parts, so some intervals are shorter.

route <- extract_to_track(
  data = haul, nc = nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom",
  statistic = c("mean", "sd", "min", "max"), output_col = "temperature"
)
head(route$samples[c(
  "sample_id", "is_interpolated", "distance_km", "temperature"
)])
#>   sample_id is_interpolated distance_km temperature
#> 1         1           FALSE   0.0000000    13.80234
#> 2         2            TRUE   0.9591421    13.80234
#> 3         3            TRUE   1.9182842    13.80067
#> 4         4            TRUE   2.8774263    13.80067
#> 5         5            TRUE   3.8365684    13.80067
#> 6         6            TRUE   4.7957105    13.80067
route$summary
#>   track_id     mean        sd      min      max  n
#> 1   haul_A 13.76075 0.0343227 13.71589 13.80234 27

An inserted position has is_interpolated = TRUE: it isn’t a new observation. We can count the recorded and inserted positions:

table(route$samples$is_interpolated)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>     3    24

This interpolates the path, not the temperature. Each inserted location takes the value of its cell, depth level and time step, as a point does. Several nearby samples can therefore get the same value.

A one-kilometre spacing can read the same grid cell several times. That is expected: these are positions along the route, not a list of unique cells. Conversely, a route can cross a narrow corner of a cell between samples without ever querying it. A smaller spacing makes this less likely, but can’t guarantee that every cell the route crosses is represented. One sample per grid cell is planned for sample_3d() (#105).

plot_track_map(route$samples, observed$samples)

Figure 1. Recorded vertices and the sampled route. Inserted positions are on an assumed path; colour shows the selected deeper temperature.

Positions between vertices follow the shortest path over the Earth’s surface (the WGS84 geodesic). Distances are horizontal; they don’t include vertical travel. A route across 180 degrees longitude takes the shorter way round.

Step 3: Understanding the summary weights

Before choosing a mean, decide what should count equally: each sampled position, each kilometre travelled, or each minute spent on the route. The same selected temperatures can give different means because these are different scientific questions.

Equal weight: what is the average sampled value?

With weighting = "equal", every sampled position gets the same weight. This is the ordinary arithmetic mean. It can be useful when each recorded observation should count equally. With irregular sampling, a densely recorded part of a track has more influence even if it represents little distance or time.

Distance weight: what conditions describe the travelled route?

With weighting = "distance", the default, a sample stands for half the distance to the previous sample plus half the distance to the next (support_km). An endpoint gets only its own half-segment. These lengths add up to the whole track length.

For example, if three consecutive samples are at 0, 1 and 4 km, their distance supports are 0.5, 2 and 1.5 km. The middle sample gets half the first kilometre plus half the next three kilometres. The weights sum to 4 km.

head(route$samples[c("sample_id", "distance_km", "support_km")])
#>   sample_id distance_km support_km
#> 1         1   0.0000000  0.4795710
#> 2         2   0.9591421  0.9591421
#> 3         3   1.9182842  0.9591421
#> 4         4   2.8774263  0.9591421
#> 5         5   3.8365684  0.9591421
#> 6         6   4.7957105  0.9591421
sum(route$samples$support_km)
#> [1] 24.93047

The mean uses those lengths as weights. This is a numerical approximation to conditions along the route.

Duration weight: what conditions describe time spent along the route?

With weighting = "duration", the same half-interval rule uses elapsed time (support_seconds). If our three samples were recorded at 10:00, 11:30 and 12:00, their supports would be 45, 60 and 15 minutes. The track spends 90 minutes in its first kilometre and only 30 minutes in its next three kilometres. A mean describing time spent should therefore differ from a mean describing distance travelled.

Durations are measured between UTC instants. A stationary animal can have positive time support even when its distance support is zero. A track whose samples all have zero weight, such as a stationary one with distance weights, gets equal weights.

The same three temperatures, three different answers

The following small example shows the weights without our Copernicus data. The temperatures are invented teaching values.

weight_example <- data.frame(
  sample = c("A", "B", "C"),
  temperature = c(10, 20, 30),
  distance_support_km = c(0.5, 2, 1.5),
  duration_support_minutes = c(45, 60, 15)
)
knitr::kable(weight_example)
sample temperature distance_support_km duration_support_minutes
A 10 0.5 45
B 20 2.0 60
C 30 1.5 15 

weight_comparison <- data.frame(
  question = c("Average sample", "Average kilometre", "Average minute"),
  weighting = c("equal", "distance", "duration"),
  mean_temperature = c(
    mean(weight_example$temperature),
    weighted.mean(weight_example$temperature,
                  weight_example$distance_support_km),
    weighted.mean(weight_example$temperature,
                  weight_example$duration_support_minutes)
  )
)
knitr::kable(weight_comparison, digits = 2)
question weighting mean_temperature
Average sample equal 20.0
Average kilometre distance 22.5
Average minute duration 17.5

Equal weighting gives 20 degrees C, distance weighting 22.5 degrees C, and duration weighting 17.5 degrees C. No temperature was changed: only what each temperature stands for in the mean.

weight_shares <- cbind(
  Equal = rep(1 / 3, 3),
  Distance = weight_example$distance_support_km /
    sum(weight_example$distance_support_km),
  Duration = weight_example$duration_support_minutes /
    sum(weight_example$duration_support_minutes)
)
barplot(
  weight_shares, beside = TRUE, col = grDevices::hcl.colors(3, "Viridis"),
  ylim = c(0, 0.75), ylab = "Share of total weight",
  legend.text = c("A: 10 C", "B: 20 C", "C: 30 C"),
  args.legend = list(x = "top", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
)

Figure 2. The three sampled temperatures receive different shares of the total weight. A, B and C are the same samples in all three comparisons.

Applying each choice to our real-data example

We already have the distance-weighted result. Compare it with equal weighting, keeping the same positions and values.

To show duration weighting, add fictional UTC times to the same three recorded positions, from 08:00 to 10:00. The first segment now takes 90 minutes and the second 30 minutes. Times between the vertices are interpolated along each segment.

equal <- extract_to_track(
  data = haul, nc = nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom", weighting = "equal",
  output_col = "temperature"
)

timed_haul <- haul
timed_haul$date <- as.POSIXct(c(
  "2026-09-20 08:00:00", "2026-09-20 09:30:00", "2026-09-20 10:00:00"
), tz = "UTC")
duration <- extract_to_track(
  timed_haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom", weighting = "duration",
  output_col = "temperature"
)
data.frame(
  weighting = c("distance", "equal", "duration"),
  mean_temperature = c(
    route$summary$mean, equal$summary$mean, duration$summary$mean
  )
)
#>   weighting mean_temperature
#> 1  distance         13.76075
#> 2     equal         13.76079
#> 3  duration         13.77446
sum(duration$samples$support_seconds) / 60
#> [1] 120
weight_spread <- diff(range(c(route$summary$mean, equal$summary$mean,
                              duration$summary$mean)))

The total duration is 120 minutes. Every sample is nearest the daily time step of 20 September, so only the weights differ between the three runs. Here the three means agree to within 0.01 degrees C, because temperature changes little along this route; the invented example above shows the difference more clearly.

"sd", "min" and "max" summarise the same samples. The standard deviation uses the same weights, with the formula of summarise_3d(). Neighbouring samples along a track are usually correlated, and densifying a track doesn’t create independent observations, so the standard deviation describes the spread of the samples, not the uncertainty of the mean.

Step 4: Checking whether the spacing is fine enough

Try several spacings and compare the summaries. If they agree, the spacing is probably fine enough for this track and field; this can’t show that every crossed cell was visited.

spacings <- c(2, 1, 0.5)
runs <- lapply(spacings, function(km) {
  extract_to_track(haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
                   spacing_km = km, method = "bottom",
                   output_col = "temperature")
})
data.frame(
  maximum_spacing_km = spacings,
  samples = vapply(runs, function(r) nrow(r$samples), integer(1)),
  mean = vapply(runs, function(r) r$summary$mean, numeric(1))
)
#>   maximum_spacing_km samples     mean
#> 1                2.0      15 13.76055
#> 2                1.0      27 13.76075
#> 3                0.5      51 13.76179
spacing_spread <- diff(range(vapply(runs, function(r) r$summary$mean,
                                    numeric(1))))

Here the means at 2, 1 and 0.5 km agree to within 0.001 degrees C, so a 1 km spacing is fine enough for this haul.

Step 5: Following a dive in depth and time

Now imagine two animal locations with different depths and times.

dive <- data.frame(
  lon = c(-0.10, 0.10), lat = c(37.98, 38.06),
  depth = c(30, 180),
  date = as.POSIXct(c("2026-09-20 00:00:00", "2026-09-21 00:00:00"),
                    tz = "UTC")
)

Between vertices, sample_3d() assumes that depth and UTC time change linearly with distance along each segment. For a segment from 20 m at 10:00 to 100 m at 11:00, its halfway position gets 60 m and 10:30. This assumes steady progress along that segment; it doesn’t say where the animal really was between observations.

Step limits add samples when a segment changes quickly in depth or time, even if it moves little horizontally. With "balanced", the limits are checked together and give one even spacing:

  1. The route is about 19.7 km long, which needs at least 10 intervals at 2 km.
  2. Depth changes by 150 m, which needs at least 15 intervals at 10 m.
  3. Time advances by 24 hours, which needs at least 24 intervals at one hour.
  4. The largest of these is 24, so the function makes 24 equal intervals: about 0.82 km, 6.25 m and one hour each, with 25 positions including the ends.

These are maximum changes, not three exact spacings that must occur together. A stationary track can still need extra samples because depth or time changes.

dive_result <- extract_to_track(
  dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", spacing_km = 2,
  depth_step_m = 10, time_step = 1, time_unit = "hours",
  output_col = "temperature"
)
head(dive_result$samples[c("lon", "lat", "depth", "date", "temperature")])
#>           lon      lat depth                date temperature
#> 1 -0.10000000 37.98000 30.00 2026-09-20 00:00:00    23.16156
#> 2 -0.09167535 37.98334 36.25 2026-09-20 01:00:00    19.16716
#> 3 -0.08334994 37.98668 42.50 2026-09-20 02:00:00    17.78095
#> 4 -0.07502378 37.99002 48.75 2026-09-20 03:00:00    16.89387
#> 5 -0.06669686 37.99336 55.00 2026-09-20 04:00:00    16.07409
#> 6 -0.05836919 37.99669 61.25 2026-09-20 05:00:00    15.91007
nrow(dive_result$samples)
#> [1] 25

With the default method = "nearest", each sample takes the level nearest its depth that has a value. time_step = 1, time_unit = "hours" sets the largest step along the assumed trajectory; it doesn’t change the time resolution of the data. Each sample is matched to the time step nearest its time, here the daily step of 20 or 21 September.

Keeping separate step cuts with merged_steps

Sometimes we want to query both sets of step positions. merged_steps keeps the distance and depth subdivision and adds the time subdivision, removing positions that coincide. For this dive, the first set has 15 intervals (10 m each) and the second 24 (one hour each). Together they give 37 positions.

merged_dive <- extract_to_track(
  dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", sampling = "merged_steps", spacing_km = 2,
  depth_step_m = 10, time_step = 1, time_unit = "hours",
  output_col = "temperature"
)
nrow(merged_dive$samples)
#> [1] 37

Both modes assume the same trajectory; the extra samples don’t add observations or reveal detail that isn’t in the grid.

balanced_hours <- as.numeric(difftime(
  dive_result$samples$date, dive$date[1], units = "hours"
))
merged_hours <- as.numeric(difftime(
  merged_dive$samples$date, dive$date[1], units = "hours"
))
old_par <- par(mar = c(4, 7, 1, 1))
plot(
  balanced_hours, rep(2, length(balanced_hours)),
  xlim = c(0, 24), ylim = c(0.5, 2.5), yaxt = "n", pch = 16,
  col = "#0072B2", xlab = "Elapsed time (hours)", ylab = ""
)
axis(2, at = c(1, 2), labels = c("Merged steps", "Balanced"), las = 1)
points(merged_hours, rep(1, length(merged_hours)), pch = 16, col = "#D55E00")

Figure 3. Each dot is a requested position on the same assumed dive. Balanced sampling uses one common hourly subdivision; merged steps also keep the ten-metre subdivision. 

par(old_par)

Calendar months and years

Seconds, minutes, hours and days are elapsed-time units; one day is 24 hours in UTC. Months and years have different lengths and must be whole numbers. For these units, the function counts whole steps from the start of each segment, and a date that doesn’t exist in a shorter month falls on its last day. For example, from 31 January 2020, monthly steps give 29 February, 31 March and 30 April. Balanced sampling keeps these dates, and divides each month evenly only where the distance or depth limits need more points.

track_explorer(dive_result$samples)

Figure 4. The assumed three-dimensional trajectory, coloured by selected model temperature. Depth is the requested path depth, not an interpolated environmental layer.

Rotate the figure and look at the hover labels. Requested depths change smoothly along the assumed route, but the selected values can change in steps, because they come from the grid’s levels and time steps. The three display axes are scaled separately for readability; the view isn’t a physical scale model of horizontal distance against depth.

Step 6: Summarising a buffer around each sample

A sample takes the value of one cell. To describe the water around the route instead, give each sample a buffer: a circle of horizontal_radius_km and a depth window of depth_radius_m above and below it. Each sample then gets the mean of the values in its buffer, weighted by the volume of each cell and level, and temperature_n, the number of values. A cell counts when the circle touches it, and a level when its slab of water overlaps the depth window, as in extract_to_buffer().

buffered <- extract_to_track(
  dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", spacing_km = 2,
  depth_step_m = 10, time_step = 1, time_unit = "hours",
  horizontal_radius_km = 3, depth_radius_m = 10,
  output_col = "temperature"
)
head(buffered$samples[c("sample_id", "depth", "temperature",
                        "temperature_n")])
#>   sample_id depth temperature temperature_n
#> 1         1 30.00    22.12714            42
#> 2         2 36.25    20.12696            42
#> 3         3 42.50    17.97879            30
#> 4         4 48.75    17.06606            30
#> 5         5 55.00    16.16729            20
#> 6         6 61.25    15.90890            20
data.frame(
  per_sample = c("value at the sample", "mean in a 3 km buffer"),
  track_mean = c(dive_result$summary$mean, buffered$summary$mean)
)
#>              per_sample track_mean
#> 1   value at the sample   15.41328
#> 2 mean in a 3 km buffer   15.43586

The track mean then averages the buffer means, weighted by distance as before. Here it differs from the mean of the values at the samples by about 0.02 degrees C. Neighbouring buffers can share grid cells, so their means aren’t independent.

Step 7: Recognising gaps and missing values

A sample takes the value of the cell that contains it, so a route that leaves the grid has values along one part and NA along the rest. One warning counts the samples that get NA. The summary uses only the samples with a value: compare n with the number of samples to see how much of the track has values.

outside <- haul[c(1, 3), ]
outside$lon[2] <- 0.4
partial <- extract_to_track(
  outside, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom"
)
#> Warning: 20 of 49 samples get NA: 20 outside the grid or without a value.
partial$summary
#>   track_id     mean  n
#> 1   haul_A 13.79701 29
nrow(partial$samples)
#> [1] 49

Here 29 of the 49 samples have a value. To drop a summary built on too little of the track, filter on n.

max_samples caps the number of positions across all tracks. If a spacing would need more, the call stops with an error instead of building a very large result:

# A one-metre spacing would need far more than 100 positions.
extract_to_track(
  haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", spacing_km = 0.001, max_samples = 100,
  method = "bottom"
)
#> Error:
#> ! Track sampling exceeds max_samples.

Checking that the route stays at sea

A connecting line isn’t necessarily a plausible marine route. Two locations can both be at sea while the shortest line between them crosses a peninsula or island, and closer samples still follow the same line. A finite temperature doesn’t prove that the route stays at sea, and an NA doesn’t prove land: it may mean the data has no value there.

extract_to_track() doesn’t yet check segments against land; this is planned for sample_3d() (#105). Until then, check the samples, or the lines between vertices, against a land polygon with sf before summarising them, and add waypoints or split the track where a connection crosses land.

Step 8: Working with LINESTRING features

Track extraction takes a table of vertices, or sf POINT features. A spatial line is converted to vertices first. sf::st_coordinates() returns one row per vertex, with X and Y coordinates and an L1 column numbering the lines, so each line becomes one track. Transform the line to longitude and latitude first, and add any dates or depths as columns of the vertex table.

line <- sf::st_sf(
  haul = "haul_A",
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(as.matrix(haul[c("lon", "lat")])),
                        crs = 4326)
)
line_vertices <- as.data.frame(
  sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(line, 4326))
)
line_vertices$date <- as.Date("2026-09-20")
line_result <- extract_to_track(
  line_vertices, nc_file, var = "thetao", lon_col = "X", lat_col = "Y",
  track_col = "L1", spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom"
)
line_result$summary
#>   track_id     mean  n
#> 1        1 13.76075 27

Split multipart lines into separate lines first, so that disconnected parts aren’t joined.

Summary

  1. We took the temperature at a trawl’s recorded vertices, and at samples along the route between them.
  2. We compared equal, distance and duration weights: they answer different questions about the same samples.
  3. We checked that the sample spacing is fine enough, followed a dive whose depth and time change, and summarised a buffer around each sample.
  4. We saw how samples off the grid are counted and left out of the summary.

Use point extraction for recorded locations and buffer extraction for the values around an observation. Track extraction adds an assumed connecting route. Environmental values aren’t interpolated, and routes aren’t checked against land yet.

Environmental data: E.U. Copernicus Marine Service Information; doi:10.48670/mds-00375. The point tutorial documents the subset, licence and preparation. The trajectories are fictional.

All arguments and defaults

Expand or collapse the complete extract_to_track() signature

This signature is generated from the current function. Arguments without a default need a value. For vectors of alternatives, the first is the default.

extract_to_track(
  # Data and sources
  data, nc, var = NULL, track_col = NULL,

  # Route sampling
  sampling = NULL, spacing_km = NULL,

  # Depth along the route
  depth_step_m = NULL,

  # Time along the route
  time_step = NULL,
  time_unit = c("hours", "minutes", "seconds", "days", "months", "years"),

  # Horizontal buffer
  horizontal_radius_km = 0,

  # Depth buffer
  depth_radius_m = 0,

  # Track summary
  statistic = "mean", weighting = c("distance", "duration", "equal"),

  # Depth selection
  method = NULL,

  # Observation and output columns
  lon_col = "lon", lat_col = "lat", depth_col = "depth", date_col = "date",
  output_col = NULL,

  # Source dimensions
  lon_dim = NULL, lat_dim = NULL, depth_dim = NULL, time_dim = NULL,

  # Temporal selection
  time_match = c("nearest", "exact"), max_time_diff = NULL,

  # Route limits
  max_samples = 100000L
)
Decision Choices, meaning and default
Data and grouping data holds the vertices (a table or sf POINT features); nc the data (a netCDF file, a series of files on one grid, an open connection or a SpatProxy). var = NULL detects the only variable; track_col = NULL reads the input as one track.
sampling "vertices" uses the recorded vertices; "balanced" spaces points evenly to meet every step limit; "merged_steps" keeps separate distance and depth cuts and time cuts. Default: vertices without a step, balanced with one.
Route steps spacing_km, depth_step_m and time_step default to NULL: no step. Give the largest horizontal distance, depth change or time between points.
time_unit "seconds", "minutes", "hours" and "days" are elapsed units (a day is 24 hours); "months" and "years" are whole UTC calendar steps, clamped at month ends. Default: "hours".
Buffers horizontal_radius_km = 0 takes the value at each sample; a positive radius summarises the values in a buffer around it, with depth_radius_m metres above and below for a variable with depth.
method Without a buffer, the depth level each sample takes: "nearest" (default; the nearest level with a value), "nearest_level" (the nearest level, even without a value), "bottom" (the deepest level with a value) or "surface".
statistic "mean" (default), "sd", "min" and "max" of each track’s samples; choose one or several.
weighting "distance" (default) weights each sample by the route length it stands for, "duration" by the time, "equal" gives each sample the same weight.
Time matching time_match = "nearest" (default) takes the nearest time step, "exact" the step equal to the sample’s time; max_time_diff caps a nearest match, in days.
Columns and dimensions lon_col, lat_col, depth_col and date_col name the vertex columns; output_col = NULL names the value column after the variable. lon_dim, lat_dim, depth_dim and time_dim override the detected netCDF dimensions.
Safety limit max_samples = 100000L caps the number of positions across all tracks.

See extract_to_track() for the output columns.
